rows.stem:
(a) Name the cell used in hearing aids and watches.
(b) Define conductivity. Why is direct current (DC) not used for the measurement of resistance of an ionic solution ?
rows.solution:
(a) The mercury cell, also called the button cell. It is used in hearing aids and watches because it delivers a constant potential difference of about \(1.35\) V throughout its life: every species in its overall reaction, \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\), is a solid or a liquid, so no ion concentration changes as the cell discharges and nothing shifts the potential.

(b) Conductivity, \(\kappa\), is the conductance of one unit volume of solution held between two platinum electrodes of unit cross-sectional area and one unit length apart. Equivalently it is the reciprocal of resistivity, \(\kappa = 1/\rho\).

Direct current is not used because it would electrolyse the solution. A steady current in one direction discharges ions at the electrodes, so the composition of the solution changes while the measurement is being made, and the products collecting on the electrodes polarise them and add a resistance of their own. Alternating current avoids both problems: it reverses many times a second, so no net electrolysis occurs and nothing accumulates.

rows.stem:
(a) Complete the equation :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{+}Cl^{-} + H-C_6H_4-NH_2 \longrightarrow}\)
(b) How will you convert chlorobenzene to p-chloroaniline ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a) is printed as a DRAWN structural equation, not as text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{N_2^{+}Cl^{-}}\), plus a second benzene ring drawn with its PARA hydrogen shown explicitly (“H —”) and \(\mathrm{NH_2}\) on the opposite carbon, over a plain arrow carrying no reagent. Both compounds are named losslessly in the stem as benzenediazonium chloride and aniline, so the row is answerable from text — but the explicit para-H is a positional cue that exists only in the drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) This is an azo coupling. Aniline's ring is strongly activated by its \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group, and in mildly acidic solution the benzenediazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile attacking the position PARA to that group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-NH_2\ (p)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
The product is p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye. Coupling works only on strongly activated rings — phenols and amines — which is why benzene itself cannot be coupled.

(b) Two steps, and the order is forced by the directing effects. Nitrate the chlorobenzene first: chlorine is ortho, para directing, so the nitro group enters mainly at the para position. Then reduce that nitro group to an amino group with tin and hydrochloric acid, which leaves the chlorine untouched.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{4\text{-}H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}Cl}\)

rows.stem:
(a) Name the disease caused by the deficiency of Vitamin A.
(b) How will you confirm the presence of carbonyl group as an aldehydic group in glucose ?
rows.solution:
(a) Deficiency of vitamin A causes xerophthalmia, a hardening of the cornea that can lead to blindness, and night blindness — the inability to see in dim light, which is the earliest sign.

(b) Treat glucose with a MILD oxidising agent, bromine water. It attacks an aldehyde group and nothing else, and it converts glucose to the six-carbon monocarboxylic acid, gluconic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
A ketonic carbonyl would not be oxidised under these conditions, so the fact that the reaction occurs — and that the product still has six carbons, so no chain has been broken — establishes that the carbonyl group in glucose is an aldehyde. That glucose reduces Tollens' reagent says the same thing.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Zn\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
(Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = +\,0{\cdot}80\) V, [log 10 = 1])
rows.solution:
Zinc is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; silver is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), so two electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\). By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}\)
\(= 1.56 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.1}{(0.01)^2} = 1.56 - 0.0295\log 10^{3}\)
\(= 1.56 - 3(0.0295) = 1.56 - 0.0885\)
\(= 1.4715\ \mathrm{V}\)

The silver term is SQUARED because two silver ions are reduced per zinc atom oxidised, which is the step most often dropped here.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a particular reaction quadruples when the temperature increases from 300 K to 320 K. Calculate the energy of activation \(\mathrm{(E_a)}\) of the reaction assuming that it does not change with temperature.
(Given : log 4 = \(0{\cdot}60\), R = \(8{\cdot}314\) \(\mathrm{JK^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The rate quadruples, so \(k_2/k_1 = 4\) and the left side is \(\log 4 = 0.60\). With \(T_1 = 300\) K and \(T_2 = 320\) K the bracket is \(\dfrac{20}{300 \times 320}\), so
\(0.60 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{300 \times 320} = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{20}{300 \times 320}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.60 \times 19.147 \times 300 \times 320}{20}\)
\(E_a = 55143.36\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(55.14\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The unit is part of the answer; the marking scheme deducts half a mark if it is wrong or missing.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{K_2[Zn(OH)_4]}\)
(b) Differentiate between a double salt and a complex.
(c) Mention the type of isomerism exhibited by the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)\,(H_2O)\,Cl_2]}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Two potassium ions outside contribute \(+2\), so the complex anion is \(-2\). Four hydroxido ligands contribute \(-4\), which leaves zinc at \(+2\). The complex is the anion, so zinc takes the \(-ate\) ending. The name is potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II).

(b) A DOUBLE SALT is an addition compound of two simple salts that exists only in the solid state: dissolve it in water and it dissociates completely into its simple ions, so nothing of its identity survives in solution. Mohr's salt, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot (NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O}\), gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\). A COMPLEX keeps its coordination sphere intact in solution: the ligands stay bound to the metal and the complex ion is what goes into solution. \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) gives \(\mathrm{K^+}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\), and no free \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) — which is why it is not poisonous although potassium cyanide is.

(c) \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)(H_2O)Cl_2]}\) exhibits geometrical isomerism, that is cis-trans isomerism. The complex is square planar, so the two chlorido ligands may lie adjacent to each other or opposite each other, giving two distinct compounds.

rows.stem:
(a) A coordination compound \(\mathrm{CrCl_3 \cdot 6H_2O}\) is mixed with excess of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, three moles of AgCl are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the coordination compound.
(b) Write the oxidation state and hybridisation of the central metal in the given complex : \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\). [Atomic number : Cr = 24]
(c) Why is \(\mathrm{[Sc(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) colourless ?
rows.solution:
(a) Three moles of silver chloride per mole of compound means all three chlorides are free in solution, so none of them is inside the coordination sphere. All six water molecules must therefore be the ligands:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\)

(b) In \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) the six ammine ligands are neutral, so the whole \(+3\) belongs to the metal: chromium is \(+3\), and \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\). With only three d electrons, three of the five \(3d\) orbitals are singly occupied and TWO are empty whatever the ligand field — so no pairing is needed and two inner orbitals are available for bonding. The hybridisation is \(d^2sp^3\), giving an inner orbital octahedral complex. This is why chromium(III) complexes are almost always \(d^2sp^3\) regardless of the ligand.

(c) Colour in these ions comes from a d-d transition, in which an electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper one. Scandium is \(+3\) here, so \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\) — the d subshell is completely EMPTY, so there is no electron to promote and no d-d transition can occur. No visible light is absorbed, and the complex is colourless. An ion with a completely FILLED d subshell, such as \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), is colourless for the mirror-image reason: there is no vacancy to promote an electron into.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
How do you convert the following ?
(a) Benzene to m-Nitroacetophenone
(b) Bromobenzene to 1-Phenylethanol
(c) But-3-en-2-one to Prop-2-en-1-oic acid
rows.solution:
(a) Benzene to m-nitroacetophenone. The ORDER of the two steps is the whole question. Acylate first: Friedel-Crafts acylation gives acetophenone, and the \(-\mathrm{COCH_3}\) group is deactivating and META directing, so the nitration that follows delivers the nitro group to the meta position.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{CH_3COCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{3\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}COCH_3}\)
Nitrating first would give nitrobenzene, which is far too deactivated to undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation at all.

(b) Bromobenzene to 1-phenylethanol. Make the Grignard reagent, add ethanal, then hydrolyse; the Grignard carbon attacks the carbonyl and the product is the secondary alcohol.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CH_3CHO}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

(c) But-3-en-2-one to prop-2-en-1-oic acid. The starting material is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-CO-CH_3}\), a methyl ketone, so sodium hypoiodite cleaves the methyl group away as iodoform and acidification leaves the acid with one carbon fewer.
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-CO-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{NaOI}} \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-COOH} + \mathrm{CHI_3}\)
Note the reagent must not touch the carbon-carbon double bond, which rules out the ordinary strong oxidants and is why the iodoform route is the one used.
